blocks.text: The **CPU (Central Processing Unit)** is the main processor of a computer and is often called its **brain**. It executes program instructions, processes data and coordinates what the rest of the computer does. The CPU is a piece of **hardware**; the big box (cabinet) that houses the computer is not the CPU.

A CPU directly understands only **machine language**: instructions written as binary digits, **0 and 1**. Programs written in high-level languages must first be translated (or run inside a suitable environment) before the CPU can carry them out.

blocks.title: Three main functional groups of the CPU
rows: Interprets instructions, generates control signals and coordinates the flow of data among the processor, memory and I/O interfaces.
Performs arithmetic, Boolean logic, comparisons and bit operations.
Very small, very fast storage locations inside the processor that hold the information being worked on right now.

blocks.title: Not CPU parts
blocks.text: A **program unit** is not a standard CPU component. **Storage unit** is an ambiguous phrase, because internal registers are different from external storage. The standard trio is always **CU, ALU and registers**.
Quick memory trick: **CU directs, ALU calculates, Registers remember** (for the moment).

sections.title: ALU and Control Unit in action

blocks.text: The ALU has two functional sections: **arithmetic** and **logic**. Arithmetic covers addition and subtraction (multiplication and division use suitable execution circuitry). Logic covers the operations **AND, OR, NOT, XOR** and comparisons such as equal to, greater than or smaller than.

Comparison results help a program make decisions, with the Control Unit using them to steer execution. Tasks such as selecting, matching and merging data are built from sequences of basic operations; there is no single ALU operation for merging.

blocks.title: Who does what
rows: AND, OR, NOT, XOR, comparing, matching
Hold operands, addresses and intermediate results

blocks.title: The ALU does not do everything
blocks.text: Not every instruction is executed by the ALU alone. Functions such as **square roots and exponentials** may use an **FPU** (floating-point unit), other specialised circuitry or software. ALU capabilities vary from processor to processor.

blocks.title: Main responsibilities of the CPU
items: Execute program instructions
Process data
Coordinate operations of the computer
Temporarily hold working information in registers (other devices such as a GPU can also do specialised processing)

blocks.title: The instruction cycle
items: Fetch
Get the next instruction from memory
Decode
Work out which operation is requested
Execute
Carry out the action with the right circuitry
Write back
Save the result when one is produced

blocks.text: The cycle repeats again and again for each instruction. Some simple descriptions fold write-back into the execute stage, which is why many books quote just three stages: **fetch, decode, execute**.
**Installing a device** is not a stage of the instruction cycle. Software installation does use CPU instructions, but it is not one of the cycle stages.

**Registers** are tiny, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU. They temporarily hold operands, instructions, addresses and intermediate results. They are generally the **fastest** storage level in the basic memory hierarchy, but they are not permanent file storage.

A register is a **sequential digital circuit**, commonly built from flip-flops, because it retains a state. A purely combinational circuit has no stored state. If an MCQ offers both, remember that 'digital circuit' is broad while 'sequential circuit' is the more specific classification.

blocks.title: Important CPU registers
rows: Main-memory address involved in a read or write
Data moving to or from memory
Working data, addresses and intermediate results

blocks.text: **MAR = where**, **MDR = what**, **PC = where is the next instruction**, **IR = the instruction itself**.

blocks.title: Accumulator and memory unit
blocks.text: The **accumulator is itself a register**, not a separate memory category; other designs use general-purpose registers for results. Some elementary diagrams use **MU** (memory unit) for internal storage, but main memory (RAM) is distinct from CPU registers. MAR identifies a main-memory location; it does not fetch a file directly from an SSD or hard disk.

A **buffer** temporarily holds data during a transfer so that devices running at different speeds can still work together. For example, a print buffer stores waiting data while a slower printer processes it. A buffer register holds a small amount of data in hardware; larger buffers can live in RAM. Buffering does not make a slow device permanently faster.

**DMA (Direct Memory Access)** lets suitable hardware move data between an **I/O device and main memory** without the CPU handling every single item. Its key benefit is **reduced CPU workload**, leaving the CPU free for other tasks.

blocks.title: How a DMA transfer goes
items: The CPU and the device driver set up (configure) the transfer.
The DMA hardware moves the data between the I/O device and main memory.
Completion or errors are reported, often with an interrupt.

blocks.title: Buffer vs DMA
rows: Holds data temporarily to absorb speed differences
Moves data with less CPU intervention
Deals with who does the copying
Can be used together with DMA
Can be used together with a buffer

blocks.text: CPU involvement in DMA is **limited, not zero** (setup and completion handling). DMA does not raise clock speed, enlarge RAM or provide permanent storage.

blocks.title: Fastest to slowest
items: Registers
Inside CPU; fastest; tiny capacity
Cache (L1, L2, L3)
Copies of data likely to be needed soon
RAM
Main working memory; largest of the three
SSD / hard disk
Secondary storage; long-term files

blocks.text: **Cache** reduces the **average memory-access time**, so the CPU spends less time waiting for slower main memory. It supplements RAM; it does not replace RAM and is not permanent file storage. RAM is the main working memory for active programs and data, generally larger but slower than cache. Files needed from secondary storage are normally brought into RAM first.

blocks.title: Cache hit and miss
rows: The requested information is available in the cache level being checked.
The information is not in that cache level, so the request moves to the next level.
L1, then L2, then L3, then RAM. If every cache level misses, data comes from main memory (usually RAM).

blocks.title: Exam corrections
blocks.text: If registers and cache are both options for the fastest storage, choose **registers**. For the largest capacity among registers, cache and RAM, choose **RAM**. A cache miss does not mean the computer restarts or stops.

'Registers, cache, RAM' is a **speed hierarchy**, not a rule that every instruction searches all registers first. Instructions explicitly choose their register operands, while ordinary memory loads go through the cache hierarchy.

**Clock speed**, clock rate and clock frequency all describe the number of **clock cycles per second**. The basic unit is the **hertz (Hz)**. A 3 GHz clock produces 3 billion cycles every second. A **clock period** is the duration of one cycle, and **frequency = 1 / period**, so a shorter period means a higher frequency.

blocks.title: Instruction-throughput terms
rows: Instructions Per Cycle: average instructions completed in one clock cycle.
Kilo Instructions Per Second: thousands of instructions per second.
Million Instructions Per Second: a traditional throughput measure.

blocks.title: Cycles are not instructions
blocks.text: One instruction can take several clock cycles, while some processors finish several instructions per cycle. So never define clock speed as 'instructions per second'. **Hz** measures frequency; **IPS, KIPS and MIPS** measure instruction throughput. Bits or bytes per second describe data transfer, not CPU clock frequency.

blocks.title: What affects performance?
items: Clock rate, IPC and processor architecture
Number of cores and cache
Memory behaviour and the workload itself
Higher GHz alone does not prove that one processor is faster than another; MIPS is not a complete comparison across architectures
There is no universal PC speed of 100 KIPS
THz is a frequency unit, not the normal clock range of ordinary high-end CPUs

blocks.text: Among monitor size, keyboard type, printer speed, mouse DPI and clock speed, only **clock speed** is directly related to CPU operation.
A **core** is a processing unit inside a processor. One physical CPU package may contain several cores. Single-core processors came before dual-core and quad-core designs.

blocks.title: Multitasking and parallel work
rows: Manages several tasks, often by switching rapidly between them (time-sharing).
Performs suitable parts of a job at the same time.
Several cores run separate instruction streams simultaneously; the benefit depends on software that can divide the work.
A system with one processing unit in the traditional model.
A system with multiple processing units.

blocks.text: A **single-core** system can still multitask through time-sharing, and a uniprocessor system can still have one CPU package with several cores.

blocks.title: RISC vs CISC
rows: Traditionally linked with more complex decoding

blocks.text: Real cost and performance depend on the implementation, so CISC is not always more expensive or slower.
A **microprocessor** implements the CPU functions on a single integrated-circuit chip. Microprocessor-based computers belong to the **fourth generation** in the conventional classification.

blocks.title: Two milestone chips
items: Intel 4004: widely recognised as the first commercially available single-chip microprocessor; a 4-bit processor.
Later (Intel)
Intel 8086: a 16-bit processor with a 16-bit word and data bus and a 20-bit physical address bus.

blocks.title: Intel 8086 numbers
rows: 2^20 bytes = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MiB (basic exam notes often call this 1 MB)

blocks.text: **4004 = 1971 = 4-bit.** **8086 = 16-bit data, 20-bit address.** Say it together: 4-4-1971.

blocks.title: Companies and their chip families
rows: Name from Integrated Electronics; desktops and laptops
Advanced Micro Devices; major Intel competitor
Systems on a chip (SoC) for Mac, including MacBook and iMac
Mainstream and flagship phones, not only budget ones
Enterprise computing; PowerPC came from the Apple-IBM-Motorola (AIM) alliance
Arm-based Grace data-centre CPU announced in April 2021

blocks.text: **Ryzen = AMD, Core i7 = Intel, M1 = Apple, Snapdragon = Qualcomm, Exynos = Samsung, Dimensity/Helio = MediaTek, Grace = NVIDIA.** These are product-design associations; designing a chip and physically fabricating it are separate activities.

**Arm** was originally **Acorn RISC Machine** and later **Advanced RISC Machines**. It began at Acorn for computer applications; mobile devices became its major use later, so it was not designed only for phones. Arm is a RISC design.

blocks.title: GPU: Graphics Processing Unit
rows: Accelerates graphics, image rendering and suitable parallel computations: gaming, video processing, AI and scientific computing.
Built into a processor or SoC.
A separate graphics processor, often on a dedicated card.
The GPU is the chip; a graphics card contains a GPU plus supporting components.
NVIDIA marketed GeForce 256 as a GPU in 1999; a simple claim that one company coined the term needs context.

blocks.title: The three basic system buses
rows: Identifies a memory location or device (where).
Carries read, write and timing signals (how and when).

blocks.text: **Cache bus** is not one of the three standard bus categories, although a particular design may have a cache interconnect.

blocks.title: Cabinet and system unit
rows: The outer enclosure of a desktop computer.
The enclosure together with the internal components.
Motherboard, CPU, RAM, storage, power supply and cooling.

blocks.text: 'CPU cabinet' is an informal phrase; the cabinet is only the box and not the processor.

blocks.title: Power and availability
rows: Switched-Mode Power Supply (also called Switch Mode Power Supply). Converts mains AC into regulated DC for the components; regulators on the motherboard adapt voltages further.
A system component, not circuitry inside the CPU chip.
Unavailable for communication with the relevant computer, network or service. It may be disconnected or not ready, and does not necessarily mean damaged.

blocks.text: Bus memory aid: **Address = Where, Data = What, Control = How/When.** SMPS: **AC in, DC out.**

blocks.title: Trap checklist
items: The CPU is hardware; the language it executes directly is machine code.
CU decodes and coordinates; ALU computes and compares; registers hold working data.
MAR holds a main-memory address, never a secondary-storage file.
Fastest to slowest: Registers, Cache, RAM. Among these, RAM is the largest and registers the smallest.
MHz and GHz measure cycles per second, not bytes or instructions.
MIPS = million instructions per second; KIPS = thousands per second; no fixed 100 KIPS applies to all PCs.
Multicore helps suitable parallel tasks, yet a single core can still multitask.
A GPU is a chip; a graphics card contains a GPU and support components.
DMA reduces continuous CPU involvement in I/O-to-memory transfers.

blocks.text: Read the exact options. 'Fastest storage' includes registers, while 'largest memory' depends on which levels are being compared; secondary storage usually has even greater capacity than RAM.

revision: CPU = Central Processing Unit; it is hardware, and it directly executes machine code (binary).
Three functional groups of the CPU: Control Unit, ALU and registers.
CU decodes and coordinates; ALU does arithmetic and logic (comparisons); registers hold working data.
Instruction cycle: Fetch, Decode, Execute (and write back a result when needed).
PC = next instruction address; IR = current instruction; MAR = memory address; MDR/MBR = data transferred.
A register is a sequential digital circuit; the accumulator is itself a register.
Memory speed order: Registers > Cache > RAM > secondary storage; RAM is the largest of the first three.
Cache lowers average access time; if all cache levels miss, data comes from main memory (RAM).
Clock speed is measured in Hz (MHz, GHz); MIPS, KIPS and IPS measure instruction throughput; IPC = instructions per cycle.
Shorter clock period means higher frequency (frequency = 1 / period).
Core counts: dual 2, quad 4, hexa 6, octa 8, deca 10; single-core CPUs came first.
RISC (Arm, RISC-V) uses simple instructions; CISC (x86) uses richer, more complex ones.
Intel 4004: 1971, 4-bit, first commercial single-chip microprocessor; Intel 8086: 16-bit data, 20-bit address, 1 MiB.
Ryzen: AMD | Core i7: Intel | M1: Apple | Snapdragon: Qualcomm | Exynos: Samsung | Dimensity/Helio: MediaTek | Grace: NVIDIA.
DMA = Direct Memory Access: moves data between I/O and main memory with less CPU work. Buses: Address, Data, Control.
SMPS (Switched-Mode Power Supply) converts mains AC to regulated DC; PowerPC came from Apple, IBM and Motorola (AIM).
